bib.title: FreshLLMs: Refreshing Large Language Models with Search Engine Augmentation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "FreshLLMs: Refreshing Large Language Models with Search Engine Augmentation", Tu Vu, Mohit Iyyer, Xuezhi Wang, Noah Constant, Jerry Wei, Jason Wei, Chris Tar, Yun-Hsuan Sung, Denny Zhou, Quoc Le, Thang Luong. Venue as printed: "Preprint" (arXiv:2310.03214v2 [cs.CL], 22 Nov 2023). First author Tu Vu: Google. Other affiliations printed: University of Massachusetts Amherst, OpenAI.

COVERAGE: 26 of 26 pages, all 83,152 extracted chars, including Appendices A-H and Tables 2-5. References (pp. 10-13) skimmed. Figures 2, 8, 9 and 10 are images, so only their captions were read.

CLAIMS (all model results: benchmarked April 26, 2023, temperature 0, 500-question test set, graded by the authors)

- claim: FreshQA has 600 questions in four categories (never-, slow-, fast-changing, false-premise), each written at one-hop or multi-hop difficulty.
  number: 600; test 125 per type (500), dev 25 per type (100), 15 demonstrations
  setup: written by NLP researchers (authors and colleagues) and Upwork freelancers at $2 per example; every example manually reviewed; dev set unused in the paper
  quote: "a test set consisting of 125 questions for each of the four broad question types (500 total examples) and a development set comprising 25 questions for each question type (100 total examples)"
  where: p3

- claim: Answers stay current through manual updates by the maintainers, and the design limits how often that is needed.
  number: questions changing more than weekly excluded
  setup: annotators also gave the year the answer last changed and a supporting URL; questions can move category over time
  quote: "we excluded questions whose answers are likely to change more frequently than once per week, and additionally incorporated the expected next review date for each question."
  where: p3

- claim: RELAXED credits a correct primary answer; STRICT also requires every claim to be accurate and current. The gap between them is the hallucination measure.
  number: more than 50K judgements; two-author agreement 99% RELAXED, 96% STRICT
  setup: agreement measured on only 100 randomly sampled answers (50 valid-premise, 50 false-premise). STRICT agreement on false-premise items is 92.0 (Table 2)
  quote: "Two authors independently evaluated a subset of 100 answers in both modes and had an agreement of 99% for RELAXED and 96% for STRICT"
  where: p4; Table 2, p17

- claim: FreshEval, a few-shot LLM judge, agrees with the human raters about as well as they agree with each other.
  number: 96.5% RELAXED, 96% STRICT (average over two raters)
  setup: same 100 answers; separate prompts per mode; given question, valid answers and response; adding retrieved evidence did not help; lowest cell is 90.0 (STRICT, false-premise, vs Rater 2)
  quote: "achieving an average agreement of 96.5% with human evaluations for RELAXED and 96% for STRICT"
  where: p4; Table 2, p17

- claim: Without search, every model is weak overall and worst on fast-changing questions.
  number: overall 0.8-32.0% STRICT, 0.8-46.4% RELAXED. GPT-4 STRICT by category: fast 12.0, slow 4.0, never 64.3, false-premise 33.9, all 28.6. RELAXED: 14.4, 35.2, 69.0, 66.9, all 46.4. ChatGPT STRICT: 7.2, 16.0, 61.9, 42.7, all 32.0
  setup: T5 770M to PaLM 540B, plus Codex, GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, GPT-4
  quote: "overall accuracy ranges from 0.8% to 32.0% under STRICT , and 0.8% to 46.4% under RELAXED"
  where: p5; Tables 3-4, pp21-22

- claim: False-premise accuracy does not improve with model size for T5 and PaLM.
  number: 0.0-1.6%; OpenAI models 25.8-42.7% STRICT, 32.3-66.9% RELAXED
  setup: as above
  quote: "using larger models does not increase accuracy for T5 and PALM (“flat scaling”), with performance within the range of 0.0% to 1.6%"
  where: p5

- claim: FreshPrompt (Google Search evidence sorted oldest to newest, plus few-shot demonstrations, one LLM call) lifts GPT-4 sharply and shrinks the STRICT-RELAXED gap.
  number: GPT-4 28.6 to 75.6 STRICT, 46.4 to 77.8 RELAXED; gap 17.8 to 2.2. GPT-3.5 26.0 to 56.0 STRICT. Comparators STRICT: Perplexity 52.2, GPT-3.5 + Self-Ask 41.6, Google Search alone 39.6
  setup: GPT-4 with 10 evidences and 5 demonstrations; GPT-3.5 with 5 evidences
  quote: "GPT-4 + FRESH PROMPT achieves absolute accuracy improvements of 47% and 31.4% over GPT-4 under STRICT and RELAXED , respectively."
  where: p7, Table 1; Table 5, p26

- claim: The number of evidences matters most; more demonstrations do not help.
  number: STRICT 61.4 (1 evidence), 70.6 (5), 75.6 (10), 77.6 (15); 15 demonstrations gives 74.6
  setup: GPT-4
  quote: "increasing this number from 1 to 5, 10, and 15 leads to corresponding overall accuracy improvements of +9.2%, +14.2%, and +16.2%"
  where: p8

- claim: An explicit premise-check instruction helps false-premise questions but costs GPT-3.5 heavily elsewhere.
  number: false-premise +23.4 (GPT-3.5) and +6.4 (GPT-4) STRICT; GPT-3.5 overall down 20.8 (56.0 to 35.2)
  setup: FreshPrompt plus "Please check if the question contains a valid premise before answering"
  quote: "decreasing overall accuracy by 20.8% and 21% under STRICT and RELAXED , respectively"
  where: p8

- claim: Chain-of-thought raises RELAXED accuracy but hallucinates more under STRICT.
  number: PaLM 540B on pre-2022 knowledge: few-shot +36.1, CoT +26.9 STRICT
  setup: 5-shot TriviaQA demonstrations
  quote: "FEW-SHOT obtains better results under STRICT , as COT introduces more room for hallucination"
  where: p5

LIMITS
- Conceded: answers go stale between maintainer updates; Google Search only; one query per question; simple English questions; no comparison with fine-tuning; Lazaridou et al. (2022) not compared, for cost.
- Not shown: no confidence intervals, with 125 questions per category. All grading was done by the authors, who also built the method. The agreement figures rest on 100 answers and are raw agreement, with no chance-corrected statistic. The model behind FreshEval is not named in the extracted text. The update cadence is "regular", never specified. The split between researcher-written and freelancer-written questions is not given. Models "may still provide accurate answers" to fast-changing questions by luck (footnote 6).
- Dated: a single snapshot from April 26, 2023 of models since superseded; footnote 7 says newer versions can browse. ChatGPT and GPT-4 showed knowledge past their stated cutoff (Appendix E).

BUILDS ON: Self-Ask (Press et al., 2022); Lazaridou et al. (2022) internet-augmented few-shot prompting; Liu et al. (2023a) for evidence ordering; chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022). Benchmarks cited as prior: TimeQA (Chen et al., 2021b), SituatedQA (Zhang & Choi, 2021), StreamingQA (Liska et al., 2022), RealTimeQA (Kasai et al., 2022), CREPE (Yu et al., 2023c), (QA)2 (Kim et al., 2023).

CODE: none. The FreshEval prompt instructions are printed verbatim in Figures 5-6 (pp18-19).

FIGURES: Figure 4, p16, "FRESH QA sample evaluation." Fifteen worked examples showing the RELAXED and STRICT verdict for each grading rule, which conveys the protocol faster than the prose. The verdict columns are icons and did not extract, so check them against the image. Alternative: Figure 1, p2, two example questions per category.

PROBLEMS
- No instructions aimed at the reader. Figures 5-7 contain grader prompts, which I treated as content.
- The introduction says "32.6% and 49.0%" for the best variant (15 evidences), while section 4.3 says 47% and 31.4% for the default. Both match the tables, but the mode order is reversed between the two sentences.
- The setup tuple is printed with five names and four values: "(o, r, a, n, m) = (10, 2, 2, 5)". m = 5 is stated separately.
- Figure 7's text extracted out of order.
